title: AI-assisted development without surrendering verification
summary: Genie Code, formerly Databricks Assistant, drafts, explains, fixes and tests; you bound the request, keep confidential material out, compute the expected result yourself and run every suggestion through a review gate.
outcomes: Name the assistant as the current and former documentation pages name it, list the context it sends to the model and the permission boundary on that context.
Keep credentials, personal data and bulk records out of a request, and record what was attached and what was withheld.
Write bounded requests to explain, draft, diagnose and test, each with the grain, counting rules and expected count that make the answer checkable.
Compute expected rows by hand, catch a many-to-many join that inflates totals, correct it at the right grain with the documented JOIN rule, and reject a fix that hides an error.
Run the review gate on a draft, a fix and a test, and keep an assistance record a reviewer can read.
startingAssumptions: The learner can read a SQL join and knows that an inner join returns matching rows and a left join keeps unmatched left rows.

Unity Catalog privileges decide what a principal (a user, group or service principal) can see and read, and SELECT is the privilege to read a table's data; the governance track's Unity Catalog lesson is optional prior reading.
No workspace, model call or AI tool is available or required; every suggestion shown is an authored teaching example.
editorialRationale: Assistant teaching fails in two opposite ways: treating the tool as forbidden, or treating its output as finished. The module names the product as its pages name it, shows what it sends and what bounds it, then spends most of its beats on the discipline that makes assistance safe: a bounded request, an expected result computed independently, a many-to-many join and a misleading explanation caught by that result, a source-supported correction, a fix rejected for hiding an error, a test whose values are the learner's, a review gate and a record. Every assistant output shown is authored and labelled, so no learner needs the tool to learn the discipline.

concepts.definition: The Databricks workspace's documented coding and data assistant, formerly Databricks Assistant, that generates, explains, fixes and runs code from a prompt plus the context it is permitted to see.
concepts.example: The pane in a notebook where an analyst asks for a revenue-by-customer query over two named tables.

concepts.definition: The table metadata, code, data samples and cell outputs the assistant sends to the model with a prompt, plus resources attached or referenced with @.
concepts.example: Attaching @sales.order_lines and @logistics.shipments so the draft uses real column names.

concepts.definition: The documented rule that the assistant accesses only data and operations the user has permission for, so its context never exceeds the user's grants.
concepts.example: A table on which the user holds no privilege contributes no metadata or samples; one the user can see but not SELECT sends no data samples.

concepts.definition: The set of items an organisation keeps out of a request whatever the model side's retention statements say: credentials, personal data, bulk records and classified material.
concepts.example: Replacing a warehouse token with a placeholder and attaching eleven synthetic rows instead of the customer export.

concepts.definition: A request that names the tables, the grain of the answer, the output columns, the rules a draft could misread and the expected row count before the model drafts anything.
concepts.example: One row per customer, amount counted once per line, quantity once per shipment, unshipped orders kept, two rows expected.

concepts.definition: Testing an assistant's explanation of code by following one concrete record through the code and comparing the intermediate rows with what the explanation asserts.
concepts.example: Tracing order 1001 shows four joined rows where the explanation implied two.

concepts.definition: The multiplication of rows when a join key matches several rows on the other side: each measure repeats once per match on the opposite side, and a key with several rows on both sides (many-to-many) repeats both sides' measures.
concepts.example: Order 1001 with two lines and two shipments yields four rows, so every amount and every quantity is counted twice.

concepts.definition: Rows, counts and totals worked out from a fixture by hand or by a separate method before a draft runs, so the draft is judged against something it did not produce.
concepts.example: Amberline revenue 650 from three order lines, computed before the draft returned 1050.

concepts.definition: The level of one row per order that both detail tables are reduced to before joining, so each measure is counted once and unmatched orders survive a left join.
concepts.example: GROUP BY order_id over order lines and over shipments, then LEFT JOIN the two results.

concepts.definition: Judging an error fix by whether the row that raised the error now carries the right value, rather than by whether the error message is gone.
concepts.example: try_cast removes the parse error and turns S5 into NULL; the explicit parse yields 2026-09-05.

concepts.definition: A list of checks, each with an expected value and the source of that value, written before the draft runs and independent of its output.
concepts.example: Rows returned 2 from the customer list; rows after the join 4 from the order count; zero NULL parsed dates.

concepts.definition: The rule that a suggestion is read as a diff, run on a fixture, compared with the expected result and recorded before it is accepted, whether it is code, a fix or a test.
concepts.example: Rejecting the inner-join draft after the fixture run returned 3750 against an expected 1670.

concepts.definition: The artefact kept beside the code that holds the bounded request, the context attached and withheld, the suggestion summary, the expected and observed results, the verdict and the correction with its source.
concepts.example: A Markdown file listing the request, 1670 expected, 3750 observed, rejected, corrected with the JOIN reference.

concepts.definition: Persistent preferences the assistant considers when generating new responses, set per user or, by workspace admins, per workspace, distinct from the facts of any one request.
concepts.example: A user instruction to always return Databricks SQL and qualify every column with its table alias.

concepts.definition: A model-provider setting undergoing removal; its existing value persists, and disabled workspaces lose agentic capabilities. Check the dated controls and availability table.
concepts.example: A security review asking which admin setting governs the assistant before analysts use it on regulated data.

concepts.definition: Genie Code execution that can plan, run and revise multistep work; review its approval configuration before giving it a task.
concepts.example: An assistant that executes a generated query against a table rather than waiting for the analyst to run it.

concepts.definition: Usage billing with a monthly allowance per user; inspect current account budgets and pricing before rollout.
concepts.example: A team lead checking the account's budget and usage controls before rolling the assistant out to forty analysts.

options.text: Databricks Assistant is the notebook feature and Genie Code works only in AI/BI dashboards.
options.rationale: The features page places Genie Code in notebooks, the SQL editor, jobs, AI/BI dashboards and the file editor, so it is not a dashboard-only tool.

options.text: Genie Code is the natural-language question tool that business users open to ask about curated tables.

questions.prompt: A draft written by the assistant references a column that does not exist in logistics.shipments, a table on which the engineer holds no privilege of any kind, not even to see its metadata. Which explanation is consistent with the documented context mechanism?

options.text: No metadata or samples for that table reached the model because context respects the engineer's Unity Catalog permissions, so the model guessed a column name.
options.rationale: Documented: the assistant can access only what the user can; with no privilege of any kind the engineer cannot see the table, so nothing about it is sent and the draft is written from the prompt text alone.

options.text: The model read the table with an administrative identity and found a hidden column.
options.rationale: The documentation states the opposite: everything sent to the model respects the user's own permissions, and no elevated identity is described.

options.text: The assistant never sends table metadata, only the prompt text, so column names are always invented.
options.rationale: The usage page lists table and column names, descriptions, samples and outputs among the context sent; invented names are the exception here, not the rule.

options.text: Column names in drafts are validated against the catalog before display, so the column must exist somewhere.
options.rationale: No such validation is documented; a draft is a proposal, and the review gate exists precisely because it can be wrong.

options.text: Confirm the cell now runs without an error.

options.text: A comparison against expected values computed independently of the draft, and a record of the request, the evidence and the verdict.
options.rationale: Plausible is not verified; the gate needs an oracle the draft did not produce and a record a reviewer can read without the chat.

options.text: Nothing; running the draft is the test.
options.rationale: A run shows the draft executes, not that it is right; the authored draft ran cleanly and returned 3750 against an expected 1670.

options.text: A second run to confirm the totals are stable.
options.rationale: Determinism is not correctness; the same many-to-many join returns the same wrong 3750 every time it runs.

options.text: A confirmation from the assistant that the logic is correct.
options.rationale: The assistant's explanation is prose about its own draft, and the authored explanation of this draft was itself misleading.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague pastes a whole notebook into the chat, including a cell that reads a warehouse token from a secret scope and a cell that prints twenty customer rows with e-mail addresses, and asks the assistant to "clean this up". Explain what to change before sending and why the retention statements do not settle it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Send the cells that need work, not the notebook. Replace the token read with a placeholder, or leave the secret-scope call out of the prompt; a credential in a prompt sits in a transcript and a history whatever the partner retains, so if it was sent it is rotated. Replace the printed customer rows with a labelled synthetic sample or column names only, because personal data is governed by the organisation's policy, not by the model side's zero-retention statement. Record in the assistance record what was attached and what was withheld, so the confidentiality review can see it.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The retention statements describe what happens after the prompt leaves; the boundary on what enters it is organisational. Asking for the clean-up cell by cell, with the offending cell's structure described in words, is an acceptable alternative.

selfQuestions.prompt: Rewrite the authored explanation ("joins each order line to its shipment and adds up the line amounts and shipped quantities per customer") so that it describes what the draft actually computes for order 1001 and for order 1004.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The draft pairs every line of an order with every shipment of the same order. Order 1001 has two lines (250 and 150) and two shipments (10 and 5), so it produces four joined rows; each amount appears twice and each quantity appears twice, contributing 800 and 30 instead of 400 and 15. Order 1004 has no shipment, so the inner join produces no row for it and its 120 is absent. The result is revenue and quantity per customer inflated by the match count on the other side, with unshipped orders missing.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The rewrite names the mechanisms the original hid: pair multiplication on both sides and inner-join exclusion. Any wording that states them with the concrete counts for 1001 and 1004 is acceptable.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague proposes SUM(DISTINCT l.amount) and SUM(DISTINCT s.shipped_qty) on the draft instead of pre-aggregating. Using the fixture, explain why that is wrong, and name the documented join behaviour the corrected query relies on.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: DISTINCT removes repeated values, not repeated pairs. On the fixture Amberline's lines are 250, 150 and 250, so SUM(DISTINCT amount) returns 400 instead of 650; Brightwater's shipments include two of 20, so SUM(DISTINCT shipped_qty) returns 30 instead of 50. It also does nothing for order 1004, which the inner join has already dropped. Reducing order lines and shipments to one row per order_id restores the order grain so each measure is counted once, and the LEFT JOIN relies on the documented behaviour that all rows of the left reference are returned with NULL where there is no match, which keeps 1004 and lets COALESCE turn its missing quantity into 0.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer shows DISTINCT failing on the fixture rather than asserting it, and ties each part of the correction to a documented rule. Demonstrating the multiplication first with COUNT(*) per order_id on each table is an acceptable addition.

selfQuestions.prompt: The assistant offers to generate a test "from the current results". Explain why you decline that framing, what you ask for instead, and which three checks you add that the draft could not have anticipated.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: A test generated from the current results asserts whatever the draft produced, so a wrong draft passes its own test; the expected values must come from the fixture worked independently. I ask for the scaffolding only: a loader for the eleven fixture rows, an assertion block that compares a result with an expected table, and a helper that prints differing rows. I fill in the expected rows myself: 650/23 and 1020/50, each with its fixture source. The three added checks: rows returned equal the customers in the fixture (2), rows reaching the final grouping equal the orders (4), and shipped_at values that parse to NULL number zero.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The reasoning separates structure, which the assistant can supply safely, from values, which must be independent, and adds invariants that catch failures a per-row comparison can miss. A uniqueness check on order_id after the join is an acceptable fourth.

selfQuestions.prompt: A reviewer opens a pull request that contains only the corrected SQL. List what they cannot tell from it, and which fields of the assistance record would answer each gap.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: From the SQL alone the reviewer cannot tell what was asked for, which the request field answers with tables, grain and expected count; whether anything confidential left the notebook, which the context field answers with what was attached and withheld; what the first draft was and why it was rejected, which the suggestion summary, the observed result (3750 and 88) and the verdict with the per-key count evidence answer; what the query was supposed to return, which the expected result with its fixture sources answers; and why the correction is right rather than merely different, which the correction field answers by citing the JOIN reference.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer works backwards from a reviewer's questions to the record's structure, showing the record is evidence a diff cannot carry. Naming the try_cast decision as a second record entry is an acceptable extension.

beats.title: The assistant has two names in the documentation and one job
beats.outcome: Name the assistant as the current and former pages name it, tell it apart from Genie Agents, and list the surfaces and features it offers.
beats.explanation: Current Databricks pages title the workspace coding assistant [[dbxfe-ai-assist-genie-code-concept|Genie Code]]; the former Databricks Assistant URLs now redirect to Genie Code pages. Inspect the destination and date. It generates, explains, fixes and runs code in notebooks, the SQL editor, jobs, AI/BI dashboards and the file editor, and answers with citations from the documentation. Genie Agents, for business users' plain-English questions, is a different feature. Notice in the third state that every feature ends at the same node: you accept.

handbook.markdown:
The current name is *Genie Code*. On 24 September 2026, the former Assistant FAQ, usage and tips URLs opened Genie Code pages. Some retrieved Google Cloud snapshots were dated June, while the current AWS pages were dated September. Use the resolved page and its date when checking a capability; an old URL name does not establish old behavior.

A different product shares part of the name. *Genie Agents*, formerly Genie spaces, let analysts curate tables so business users can ask questions in plain English. Keep them apart in notes and requests.

The features matter because each fails differently. **Chat** returns prose plus citations: follow the citation, because the prose may paraphrase it wrongly. **Inline suggestions** are cheap to accept without reading. **Quick Fix** offers an accept-and-run control for basic errors, which is how a fix that silences an error reaches a notebook. **Diagnose Error** handles harder failures, including environment errors. **Slash commands** wrap common prompts. The current AWS Agent mode page describes configurable execution approvals. Check those controls before beginning work.

What this beat does not claim: menu placement, which model answers, or availability on your cloud and tier. Everything shown as assistant output in this module is authored and labelled; no response was captured.

beats.recap: Genie Code is the current coding assistant; former Assistant URLs redirect, and Genie Agents serves a separate data-question use case.
beats.changeNote: Primary-source closeout corrects redirects, mode and approval behavior on 2026-09-24.

beats.title: The model sees what you can see, and nothing you cannot
beats.outcome: List the context the assistant sends with a prompt and predict what happens when a named table is outside your grants.
beats.explanation: To complete a task the assistant sends your prompt and relevant [[dbxfe-ai-assist-context-concept|context]] to the model: table and column names, descriptions, the code you are working with, data samples and cell outputs, plus anything you attach or reference with @. Everything sent respects your [[dbxfe-ai-assist-permission-concept|Unity Catalog permissions]]: without SELECT no data samples from a table are sent, and a table you hold no privilege on contributes nothing. Notice in the second state that the request still goes through; the excluded table never enters the context, and the draft is written without it. That is one source of a confident, wrong draft.

samajh.text: Socho tum ek research library mein ho jahan har shelf ke liye alag card chahiye. Tum librarian se bolte ho, 'is topic pe summary likh do.' Woh sirf un shelves se kitaabein uthayega jinke card tumhare paas hain. Jo shelf tumhare card se nahi khulti, usme woh jhaank bhi nahi sakta, chahe tum kitna bhi bolo. Aur agar zaroori kitaab usi band shelf pe hai, to summary confident lagegi par adhoori hogi.
samajh.mapping: The librarian is the model behind the assistant, your cards are Unity Catalog grants, the shelves are tables, and the summary is the draft.
samajh.boundary: The assistant also receives code, samples, outputs and instruction files you did not mention; a library-card picture says nothing about what you paste into the request yourself.

handbook.markdown:
The usage page lists what the assistant sends to the model, and the list answers two questions at once. For a better draft: attach the tables, notebooks, queries or files the answer depends on, with the pane's Add context control or by typing `@resource_name`, so the model works from real column names and descriptions rather than your paraphrase; the tips page adds that documented tables and columns in Unity Catalog improve answers. For confidentiality: the same list says what already leaves the notebook when you press Enter, including cell outputs you may have forgotten are on screen and samples from tables you reference. Instruction files count too: the Google Cloud custom-instructions page, as the author recalled it (only its title and snippet were re-confirmed in this build), says Genie Code reads AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files found up the directory tree of the open notebook and injects them into its context; confirm the page for your cloud and release.

The permission boundary is documented plainly: the assistant can only access data and perform operations you have permission for, and all data sent to the model respects your Unity Catalog permissions. Read it precisely: the pages promise that no data you cannot access is sent, and Unity Catalog governs seeing an object's metadata separately from reading its data. Without SELECT no data samples from a table are sent, but if you can still see its metadata, as its owner or through a discovery privilege such as BROWSE where enabled (see the governance module's privileges reference), its names may reach the model. For a table you hold no privilege on, two consequences follow. A draft over it is written from the prompt text alone and may name a column that does not exist; the remedy is a grant, not a cleverer prompt. And the assistant cannot read around a denial, because it never sees more than you do.

The trust page covers the model side: partners retain nothing, even for abuse monitoring, and submissions are not used to train generative foundation models Databricks offers to third parties. What should enter the prompt is the next beat. What this beat cannot say: how many sample rows are sent, or how context is condensed before it reaches the model.

beats.recap: Prompt plus metadata, code, samples, outputs and instruction files, bounded by your own grants; an ungranted table is silently absent.

beats.title: Zero retention is a fact about the partner, not a licence to paste
beats.outcome: Decide, item by item, what enters an assistant request and name a substitute for each thing withheld.
beats.explanation: The trust page says model partners do not retain submitted data, even for abuse monitoring, and that submissions are not used to train generative foundation models Databricks offers to third parties. That bounds what happens after the prompt leaves; it says nothing about what belongs in the prompt. A token pasted into a chat sits in a transcript; a customer's personal data in a sample may breach a policy the platform never sees. The [[dbxfe-ai-assist-confidential-concept|confidentiality boundary]] is yours. Notice in the table that every withheld item has a substitute that still gets a useful draft.

handbook.markdown:
Quote the retention statements exactly to a security reviewer, because their scope matters. Partners do not retain data submitted through AI assistive features, even for abuse monitoring, and partner-powered features use zero-data-retention endpoints. Databricks does not use submitted data, prompts or responses to train generative foundation models that it makes available to third parties. Content filtering or the model provider's own safety mechanisms apply. None of that is a reason to paste a credential. The prompt also lives in your browser, in the pane's conversation history, in a colleague's screenshot and in the assistance record you are about to write. A secret that has been in a prompt is a secret to rotate.

A practical classification, written before the first request and kept in the record: **attach** table references and small labelled samples, because the model works better from real names; **withhold** contact and identity columns, bulk exports and anything your policy classifies, replacing them with column names or synthetic rows; **never** send credentials, tokens, connection strings or private keys, replacing them with placeholders the draft can keep. Error text is usually safe once internal hostnames and paths are shortened. Instruction files the assistant reads automatically belong on the same list: keep secrets out of them.

The substitute column is the point. Withholding rarely costs draft quality: a placeholder token drafts the same code, and eleven synthetic rows show the same shape. What this beat cannot decide is your organisation's policy; it gives the questions and a place, the record, to write the answers. Administrators also control the partner-powered setting behind these features, which an extension card covers.

beats.recap: Retention statements describe the model side; what enters the prompt is your decision, item by item, with a substitute for each thing withheld.

beats.title: A bounded request names the grain before the model guesses it
beats.outcome: Write a request for a transformation that states tables, grain, counting rules and the expected row count.
beats.explanation: The tips page asks for specific prompts, a stated response structure and attached context. A [[dbxfe-ai-assist-bounded-concept|bounded request]] adds what wrong drafts most often miss: the grain, the counting rule for tables with several rows per key, and the expected row count. 'Revenue by customer' leaves the model to decide how order lines and shipments meet; the bounded version says each amount counts once per line, each quantity once per shipment, and two rows are expected. Notice in the comparison that every open guess is a place a draft can be wrong without looking wrong.
beats.hint: Ask which parts of the request a wrong draft could still satisfy.

handbook.markdown:
A bounded request has five parts, and each narrows the next. **Tables**, attached or @-referenced, so the draft uses real names. **Grain**: one row per what. **Columns** with definitions, including which table each measure comes from: 'revenue = SUM(order_lines.amount), shipped_qty = SUM(shipments.shipped_qty)' already tells the model that neither table may multiply the other. **Rules the draft could misread**: an order may have several lines and zero or many shipments; keep unshipped orders; shipped_at arrives as text. **Expected shape on a fixture**: two rows, and the expected totals if you have them. The tips pages add response structure: ask for the SQL only, or numbered steps, so the answer is easy to diff.

The same shape serves the other three uses. **Explain**: 'Explain what this cell computes for order 1001, step by step, giving the number of rows after each clause.' A step-by-step answer about a named record produces claims you can trace. **Diagnose**: paste the redacted error text, say what the cell was meant to do, and ask for the cause before any fix. **Test**: 'Write a pytest fixture that loads these eleven rows and a helper that compares a result DataFrame with an expected one; leave the expected values as placeholders.'

A bounded request does not make the answer right; it makes a wrong answer visible. An eight-row join against 'four orders, two customers' fails before anyone reads the SQL. Conversation history lets a follow-up correct a previous answer without restating everything, but restate the grain whenever it changes. Custom instructions, covered in an extension card, carry standing preferences; the request carries the facts of this task.

beats.recap: Tables, grain, columns, counting rules and the expected count: a bounded request makes a wrong draft visibly wrong.

beats.title: An explanation is a claim about the code, tested by one record
beats.outcome: Turn an assistant's explanation into checkable claims and test them by tracing one record.
beats.explanation: Asking the assistant to explain a cell returns prose, and prose can sound complete and be wrong. The authored explanation says the draft 'joins each order line to its shipment and adds up the line amounts and shipped quantities per customer'. Trace order 1001: two lines and two shipments, so the join emits four rows and every amount and quantity appears twice. 'Its shipment' hides the multiplication; 'per customer' hides that order 1004, with no shipment, is absent. An [[dbxfe-ai-assist-explain-concept|explanation check]] is one record followed step by step. Notice in the trace where the words and the rows part company.

samajh.text: Socho koi dost tumhe raasta batata hai: 'seedha jao, ek hi mod hai, phir bazaar aa jayega.' Sunne mein perfect. Par ek baar khud chal ke dekho: jahan woh 'ek mod' bola tha, wahan do raste nikalte hain, aur dono pe bazaar ka board laga hai. Dost jhooth nahi bol raha tha; usne raasta yaad se bataya, zameen se nahi. Explanation bhi aisi hi hai: sunne mein poori, chalne pe adhoori.
samajh.mapping: The friend's directions are the assistant's explanation, walking the route once is tracing one record through the query, and the fork with two boards is the extra joined rows for order 1001.
samajh.boundary: A route has one truth on the ground; a query's behaviour depends on the data it meets, so one traced record can prove an explanation wrong but cannot prove it right for every record.

handbook.markdown:
Chat answers come with citations; the citation is the part to trust, because it points at a page you can read, while the prose is the model's paraphrase of your code. Treat each phrase as a claim with an implied row count, then pick a record whose behaviour would differ if the claim were false. For this draft, order 1001 is that record: two lines and two shipments, so 'each order line to its shipment' predicts two joined rows and the data produces four. Order 1004 tests the last phrase: no shipment, so 'total revenue per customer' predicts inclusion and the inner join produces nothing.

The trace itself is mechanical. Write the clauses in execution order: FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, SELECT. For the chosen record, note the number of rows after each clause and what each row carries. A join emits one row per matching pair, so a key with two rows on each side yields four; a WHERE drops rows; a GROUP BY collapses them, and the aggregate reads every surviving row. The moment a count differs from the explanation's implication, the explanation is wrong, whatever it says next.

The explanation here was authored for this module, not captured, and a real response may well be correct; the method does not depend on the assistant being wrong. It depends on treating an explanation as a hypothesis. When the trace agrees, you have one confirmed record, not a proof: choose a second record that exercises a different branch, such as an order with one line and three shipments, before relying on the explanation. A useful follow-up request is 'give the row count after each clause for order 1001', which turns the prose into numbers you can compare.

beats.recap: An explanation is prose about code; one traced record shows whether its implied row counts survive contact with data.

beats.title: A many-to-many join multiplies both sides' measures
beats.outcome: Predict the output of a draft whose join key has several rows on both sides and identify which measures are inflated and by how much.
beats.explanation: The authored draft joins order lines to shipments on order_id and sums amount and shipped_qty per customer. An inner join returns every matching pair. Order 1001 has two lines and two shipments, a many-to-many match: four rows, so each amount and each quantity counts twice. Order 1003 has one line and three shipments: 900 counts three times, while its quantities are right. Order 1004 has no shipment and vanishes. This is [[dbxfe-ai-assist-fanout-concept|join fan-out]]: a measure repeats once per match on the other side. Notice in the matches table which multiplier each measure receives.
beats.hint: Multiply lines by shipments for each order before you add anything up.

handbook.markdown:
The JOIN reference states the mechanism plainly: an inner join returns the rows that have matching values in both table references. 'Rows' means pairs. When order_id 1001 has two rows in order_lines and two in shipments, the join emits 2 × 2 = 4 rows. Each row carries one line's amount and one shipment's quantity, so SUM(amount) reads each line once per matching shipment and SUM(shipped_qty) reads each shipment once per matching line. That is the signature of many-to-many: both sides inflate. Order 1003 is one-to-many, one line and three shipments, so only the amount inflates. A draft can therefore be half right, as Brightwater's quantity is, and pass a casual glance.

The authored draft:

```sql
SELECT l.customer,
       SUM(l.amount) AS revenue,
       SUM(s.shipped_qty) AS shipped_qty
FROM sales.order_lines l
JOIN logistics.shipments s ON l.order_id = s.order_id
GROUP BY l.customer;
```

Two cheap checks expose it before any total is read. Count the joined rows and compare with the number of orders: 8 against 4. Then count rows per key on each side:

```sql
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM sales.order_lines GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;   -- 1001 (2)
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM logistics.shipments GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; -- 1001 (2), 1003 (3)
```

A key that appears in both results is many-to-many and inflates both measures; a key in one result inflates the other side's measure. The checks also name the correction: every side with repeats is aggregated to order_id before the join. The inner join's other effect is silent: 1004 has no pair, so its 120 disappears. Fan-out is not specific to Databricks, SQL or assistants; a pandas merge and a Spark DataFrame join behave the same way.

beats.recap: Every matching pair is a row; each measure repeats once per match on the other side, so 1670 becomes 3750 and 73 becomes 88.

beats.title: Compute the expected result before the draft can tell you what to expect
beats.outcome: Produce an expected-result table from a fixture, with a source for each value and a count check, before running a draft.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-ai-assist-expected-concept|independent expected result]] is worked out from the fixture before the draft runs, by hand or by a separate method, so the draft is judged against something it did not produce. Revenue belongs to order lines: 250 + 150 + 250 = 650 and 900 + 120 = 1020, total 1670. Quantity belongs to shipments: 23 and 50, total 73. Two rows. Add the count that catches partial failures: rows reaching the final grouping should equal orders, 4. Notice in the third state that the draft's 8 rows fail this check before any total is compared.

handbook.markdown:
The expected result is the oracle, and an oracle has one rule: it must not come from the thing under test. Reading the draft's first output and saving it as the baseline produces a test that detects future change, not present error; the authored draft would pass its own baseline at 3750. So the values come from the fixture by hand, or from a second method that shares no logic with the draft: a spreadsheet, a query over one table at a time, a colleague's independent calculation, or the finance total computed from order lines alone.

Work each measure at its own table. Revenue belongs to order lines, so sum the line rows and never look at shipments: 650 and 1020. Quantity belongs to shipments, so sum the shipment rows through each order's customer: 23 and 50. Write the row count and the grand totals as separate expected values, because a per-row match can hide a missing customer and a grand total can hide two errors that cancel.

Add structural checks the draft cannot have anticipated. The rows reaching the final grouping should equal the number of orders, because both measures are meant to be counted at order grain: 4. Each order_id should appear once there. No shipped_at should parse to NULL. These are cheap to state and they fail first, which is why the third state puts the count before the totals.

Name the source of every expected value. A mismatch then points at evidence, and a reviewer can recompute the oracle instead of trusting it. What the oracle cannot do is prove the query on production data: a fixture with no duplicate shipment rows says nothing about a table that has them, which is why the assistance record lists that as unverified.

beats.recap: Expected rows come from the fixture, never from the draft; name each value's source and add count checks that fail before the totals.

beats.title: Correct at the grain, then cite the rule that makes it right
beats.outcome: Correct a many-to-many join by reducing both sides to the join key's grain and justify each move with the documented join semantics.
beats.explanation: The fix is not a DISTINCT somewhere; it is restoring the [[dbxfe-ai-assist-grain-concept|order grain]] on both sides before they meet. Reduce order lines to one row per order_id, reduce shipments to one row per order_id, then LEFT JOIN the two and sum per customer. The documented JOIN semantics support each move: an inner join returns every matching pair, which is why the draft multiplied, and a left join returns all rows of the left reference with NULL where there is no match, which is why order 1004 survives. Notice in the corrected plan that no detail table meets another.

samajh.text: Shaadi mein do register hain: ek mein har family ke mehmaan, doosre mein har family ke gifts. Kisi ne dono ko family naam se jod diya, har mehmaan har gift ke saath ek line mein. Sharma family ke do mehmaan aur do gifts se chaar lines ban gayi: mehmaan double gine gaye, gifts bhi double. Sahi tareeka: pehle har register mein family-wise total nikalo, phir dono totals ek line mein rakho. Jo family gift nahi laayi, uski line bhi rakho, gift ki jagah zero.
samajh.mapping: The two registers are order_lines and shipments, the family is the order_id, the four pairwise lines are the many-to-many join, the family-wise totals are the two pre-aggregations, and keeping the family with no gift is the LEFT JOIN with COALESCE.
samajh.boundary: A family name is unique in the story; in data the key can also be duplicated by mistake inside one table, which is why the test plan still checks one row per order after the join.

handbook.markdown:
The corrected query:

```sql
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer, SUM(amount) AS amount
  FROM sales.order_lines
  GROUP BY order_id, customer
),
shipped AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(shipped_qty) AS shipped_qty
  FROM logistics.shipments
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.customer,
       SUM(o.amount) AS revenue,
       SUM(COALESCE(s.shipped_qty, 0)) AS shipped_qty
FROM order_totals o
LEFT JOIN shipped s ON o.order_id = s.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer;
```

Each decision has a reason you can cite. The two common table expressions reduce each detail table to order grain, so order_id is unique on both sides and the JOIN reference's 'matching values' produce at most one pair per order. LEFT JOIN, documented as returning all rows of the left reference with NULL where there is no match, keeps order 1004 and its 120. COALESCE turns that NULL quantity into 0 so the sum is defined. On the fixture the result is 650 / 23 and 1020 / 50, two rows, totals 1670 and 73: the expected table exactly. Grouping order_totals by customer as well assumes one customer per order; add that as a check rather than trusting it.

Alternatives and their limits. SUM(DISTINCT amount) removes repeated values, not repeated pairs: on this fixture Amberline's two 250 lines collapse and it returns 400, and SUM(DISTINCT shipped_qty) collapses S4 and S5 for Brightwater. Pre-aggregating shipments alone is the tempting half-fix: with the draft's inner join revenue reads 1550, because order 1004 is still lost, and only with a LEFT JOIN as well does it match finance at 1670; either way each of 1001's two lines still carries the order's 15 shipped units, so Amberline's quantity reads 38. A window that keeps one shipment per order fixes the amount but throws away quantities. Aggregating each table to customer grain separately and joining the two results is also correct.

The move generalises: whenever measures are summed across a join, every side must be at the grain of the join key, or reduced to it first. A reviewer who doubts the fix reads the JOIN page, not your chat history.

beats.recap: Reduce every side with repeats to the join key's grain, LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched rows, sum once; cite the JOIN reference for both moves.

beats.title: A fix that silences an error can change the answer in silence
beats.outcome: Judge a suggested error fix by the row that raised the error rather than by the disappearance of the message.
beats.explanation: Quick Fix proposes a correction for a basic error that you can accept and run; Diagnose Error analyses harder ones. Neither checks the result. The authored case: a quarter filter casts shipped_at to DATE and fails on S5, which reads 2026/09/05. A suggested fix swaps CAST for try_cast. The error disappears because try_cast returns NULL instead of raising on malformed input, so S5 becomes NULL, fails the filter and takes 20 units with it. The [[dbxfe-ai-assist-diagnose-concept|cause-versus-symptom check]] reads the row that raised the error. Notice in the timeline where the two fixes diverge.

handbook.markdown:
Errors are where assistance is most tempting and least checked, because the goal shifts from 'right answer' to 'make it run'. The documented tools help with the first half: Diagnose Error reads the failure and names a likely cause, including environment errors; Quick Fix proposes a small edit with an accept-and-run control. Deciding whether the edit resolves the cause is yours.

The authored case has the common shape. The quarter cell filters shipments with `CAST(shipped_at AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE'2026-07-01' AND DATE'2026-09-30'`. S5 holds `2026/09/05`, which the cast does not accept, and with ANSI_MODE on, the documented default for accounts created on or after 19 October 2022, the cast raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT. try_cast is documented to return NULL instead of an invalid-data error, so swapping it in makes the cell succeed and turns S5 into NULL. A BETWEEN over NULL is never true, so S5 and its 20 units leave the result without a message: Brightwater's quarter quantity reads 30 against an expected 50, and only the expected table notices. Check your own warehouse's setting before predicting a cast; a session can change it.

The fix that resolves the cause parses each format on purpose, for example `CASE WHEN shipped_at LIKE '____/__/__' THEN to_date(shipped_at, 'yyyy/MM/dd') ELSE to_date(shipped_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd') END`, and adds a check to the test plan: rows where the parsed date is NULL while the source text is not must number zero. The check is the durable part; a third format would fail again, which is the behaviour you want.

A rule for any suggested fix: find the row that raised the error, run the fixed code on the fixture, and read that row's value. If it is right, the cause is resolved; if it is NULL, dropped or defaulted, the fix hid the cause. Widened types, try_ functions, swallowed exceptions and added filters are the usual suspects.

beats.recap: Find the row that raised the error and read its value after the fix; a NULL where a date belongs means the error moved into the data.

beats.title: Ask for the test's scaffolding; write its expected values yourself
beats.outcome: Construct a test with the assistant's help while keeping every expected value independent of the draft.
beats.explanation: The assistant can construct a test: a fixture loader, an assertion block, a comparison helper. What it must not supply is the expected values, because a test that asserts the draft's current output is a snapshot of whatever the draft did, wrong included. A [[dbxfe-ai-assist-testplan-concept|test plan]] lists each check with its expected value and the source of that value: 650 from the lines of orders 1001 and 1002, row count 2 from the customer list, 4 rows after the join from the order count, zero NULL dates. Notice in the second state which checks the suggested versions pass, and why.

handbook.markdown:
Split the test into the part the assistant can write safely and the part it cannot. Safe: loading the eleven fixture rows into two temporary views or DataFrames, a helper that compares a result with an expected table and prints differing rows, and the assertion boilerplate. Not safe: the expected table, the counts, the totals and the invariants, because the model can only take those from your prompt, from its own draft, or from a guess, and two of the three are worthless.

A test plan in the record has three columns before the run: the check, the expected value and the source of that value. After the run it gains observed and verdict columns. Against the fixture the suggested versions fail five of seven. The two they pass are instructive: rows returned, because grouping by customer always yields two rows, and Brightwater's quantity, because order 1003 has one line, so nothing repeats its shipments. Those are exactly the checks a casual reader tries first, which is why the plan has seven.

A sketch of the scaffolding in PySpark, with the values filled in by you:

```python
expected = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("Amberline Motors", 650, 23), ("Brightwater Pumps", 1020, 50)],
    "customer string, revenue long, shipped_qty long")
result = spark.sql(corrected_sql)
assert result.count() == 2
assert result.exceptAll(expected).count() == 0
assert expected.exceptAll(result).count() == 0
```

The two exceptAll checks together make the comparison symmetric, so a missing row and an extra row both fail. Run it on the fixture, not on production, and keep it beside the query so the next change runs the same oracle. A fixture test cannot prove the query on data the fixture does not contain; say so in the record.

beats.recap: Scaffolding from the assistant, values from the fixture; a test plan names each check, its expected value and where that value came from.

beats.title: Accepting a suggestion is a code review you sign
beats.outcome: Apply the same five-step gate to a draft, a fix and a test, and say what the accept-and-run shortcut omits.
beats.explanation: Accept and run is one click; the [[dbxfe-ai-assist-review-concept|review gate]] makes it a decision. Read the diff: a changed filter or a dropped column shows there. Run it on the fixture. Compare with the expected result. Record the request, the verdict and the evidence. Then accept or reject. The gate is the same for a draft, a quick fix and a generated test, and it matters more when the assistant can run code for you: the result is still yours to answer for. Notice in the second state that the shortcut skips exactly the steps that produce evidence.

handbook.markdown:
The gate has five steps because each catches a different failure. **Read the diff** catches changes the request did not ask for: a quick fix that also removed a WHERE clause, a draft that renamed a column, a test that asserts the draft's own output. Read it as a diff against the previous cell, not as fresh code, because the eye forgives fresh code. **Run on the fixture** makes the behaviour concrete on eleven rows you can hold in your head, and it costs seconds. **Compare with expected** uses the oracle from the expected-result beat; counts first, because they fail fastest. **Record** writes the request, the suggestion summary, the observed result and the verdict into the assistance record before the decision, so a rejection leaves as much evidence as an acceptance. **Accept or reject** is then a sentence you can defend.

The shortcut is not laziness; it is the product's convenience. Quick Fix offers accept and run because many basic fixes are right, and the offer is useful. The gate is the habit that makes the offer safe: the fixture run and the comparison sit between the click and the notebook.

The documentation also describes an assistant that plans and runs multistep tasks itself, with configurable approvals and Auto-approve as the current AWS first-use default. Auto-approve is not a security boundary; choose the approval setting before starting. The agent extension card explains what changes: nothing in the steps, everything in their timing, because the gate must precede permission to execute. Two things the gate does not do: it does not certify production data, and it does not evaluate the model. It reviews one change, on one fixture, against one oracle, and says so.

beats.recap: Read the diff, run on the fixture, compare with expected, record, then accept; accept-and-run skips the four steps that make evidence.

beats.title: Keep the request, the evidence and the verdict together
beats.outcome: Write an assistance record that lets a reviewer who was not in the chat see what was asked, what was checked and why the result was accepted.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-ai-assist-record-concept|assistance record]] is the artefact that makes assisted work reviewable: the bounded request, the context attached and withheld, a summary of the suggestion, the expected result with the source of each value, the observed result, the verdict, and the correction with the documentation it rests on. It lives beside the code in version control, not in a chat history. Notice in the second state that the same shape holds an error fix: the evidence changes, the fields do not, so a reviewer reads both the same way.

Do tarah ki garage hoti hain: ek jahan sirf bill milta hai, aur ek jahan job card milta hai, jisme likha hota hai kya complaint thi, kya check kiya, kya reading aayi, kya badla, kya nahi badla aur kyun. Doosri garage pe agla mechanic bhi kaam samajh leta hai bina pehle wale se baat kiye. Assistance record wahi job card hai.
samajh.mapping: The complaint is the bounded request, the readings are the expected and observed results, the parts changed are the correction, and the next mechanic is the reviewer who was not in the chat.
samajh.boundary: A job card records work already done; the assistance record also records what was withheld from the request, which no garage form asks for.

handbook.markdown:
A pull request that contains only the corrected SQL tells a reviewer what the code is and nothing about why it is right. The record fills the gap with seven fields, each answering a question the reviewer would otherwise ask in person. *Request*: what was asked, with grain and expected count, so the reviewer knows what 'correct' meant. *Context*: what was attached and what was withheld, so the confidentiality review is a read rather than an interview. *Suggestion*: one line, labelled authored in this module and labelled with its source in real work; never the whole transcript as evidence, because a transcript is prose. *Expected*: the table with sources. *Observed*: what the fixture run returned. *Verdict*: accepted or rejected, with the evidence that decided it. *Correction*: what changed and the documentation it rests on.

Keep it as a Markdown file beside the query, or as a section of the pull request description, with the fixture and the test next to it. A chat history is not a substitute: it may not persist, it belongs to one user, and it mixes the request with everything else said that day. A reviewer who doubts the JOIN reasoning follows the citation in the correction field, not a link to a conversation.

The record is also where unverified items live. 'Production may contain duplicate shipment rows the fixture lacks' is a sentence that protects the next person; leaving it out turns a fixture pass into an implied production guarantee. A few entries into the habit, the record becomes the first place a team looks when a number is questioned, which is the point.

beats.recap: Seven fields beside the code: request, context, suggestion, expected, observed, verdict, correction; a chat history is not a record.

extensionCards.prompt: What do custom instructions change, and which suggestions do they not reach?
extensionCards.answer: They set standing preferences the assistant considers for new responses, per user or per workspace; they do not reach Quick Fix or Autocomplete, and they never supply a request's grain or expected count.
extensionCards.explanation: The Google Cloud custom-instructions page, as the author recalled it (only its title and snippet were re-confirmed in this build; confirm the page for your cloud and release), documents two kinds of [[dbxfe-ai-assist-extension-instructions-concept|custom instructions]]: user instructions in a .assistant_instructions.md file in your workspace folder, and workspace instructions that only workspace admins edit and that generally take priority. They apply to every response except Quick Fix and Autocomplete, so the fixes you are most tempted to accept in one click are the ones your instructions do not shape. Per the same page, Genie Code also reads AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files up the directory tree, which makes every instruction file part of the context and therefore subject to the what-not-to-paste rule. An instruction such as 'always return Databricks SQL and qualify every column' removes small corrections; it cannot know that two rows are expected on today's fixture.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Separates persistent preferences from per-request facts and shows that the one-click fixes bypass instructions entirely.

recap.title: Ask freely, verify independently, record everything
recap.markdown: **The assistant proposes; you verify against something it did not produce.** Genie Code, formerly Databricks Assistant, sends your prompt with permission-bounded context to a model and hands back a draft, an explanation, a fix or a test. A bounded request fixes the grain, the counting rules and the expected count before the model guesses them; the confidentiality boundary decides what enters the prompt whatever the partner retains. An expected result computed by hand from a fixture is the oracle: it caught a many-to-many join whose every row was right and whose row count was wrong, inflating 1670 to 3750 and 73 to 88. Correct at the grain, cite the JOIN rule, reject a fix that trades an error for a silent NULL, and keep the request, the evidence and the verdict together where a reviewer can read them. **Transfer challenge:** take a query an assistant drafted for you, write the bounded request it should have had, compute three expected values by hand from a ten-row fixture, and run the review gate on it as if it were new.

appliedTask.title: Price order lines without letting the price list multiply them
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline now re-prices order lines against `ref.price_list` (part_id, price, effective_from), which holds several dated prices per part; `sales.order_lines` also carries part_id, qty and the order's order_date. Fixture: line 1001-1 (P1, qty 2), line 1001-2 (P2, qty 1), line 1002-1 (P1, qty 3), both orders dated 2026-09-10; prices P1 10 from 2026-01-01, P1 12 from 2026-07-01, P2 5 from 2026-01-01. An authored assistant draft joins lines to the price list on part_id and sums qty × price per order. Write the bounded request you would send, the test plan with expected rows computed by hand, what the draft returns and why, and the corrected SQL.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Request: "One row per order over @sales.order_lines and @ref.price_list: order_value = SUM(qty × price), where price is the single price_list row for the part whose effective_from is the latest on or before the line's order_date; parts have several dated prices; two rows expected on the fixture; return the SQL only." Expected by hand: on 2026-09-10 P1 costs 12 (the 2026-07-01 row) and P2 costs 5, so order 1001 = 2 × 12 + 1 × 5 = 29 and order 1002 = 3 × 12 = 36; two rows; total 65. Test plan: rows returned 2 (orders in the fixture); 1001 = 29 and 1002 = 36 (hand computation); priced rows = 3 (one per line); no line with a NULL price. The draft pairs each line with every price row for its part, a many-to-many on part_id: line 1001-1 meets both P1 prices, 2 × 10 + 2 × 12 = 44, plus 5 gives 1001 = 49; line 1002-1 gives 30 + 36 = 66; it fails both value checks and the priced-rows check (5 against 3). Corrected: join lines to prices on part_id with effective_from <= order_date, rank the matches per line by effective_from descending, keep rank 1, then SUM(qty × price) per order. Observed on the fixture: 29 and 36, two rows, three priced rows. The JOIN reference explains the multiplication; the correction restores line grain before summing.
appliedTask.reasoning: The task moves the fan-out from detail rows to versioned reference rows, so the learner must recognise the same mechanism in a different table and add a grain check, one priced row per line, that the earlier fixture did not need. Ranking by effective date is one acceptable correction; a correlated subquery for the latest effective_from on or before the order date is another.
